newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe intervenes in Zimbabwe cellphone battle.
newsitem.headline: Mugabe intervenes in Zimbabwe cellphone battle.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe has ordered his ministry of telecommunications to licence a private company that has been battling the state in the courts for the last three years for permission to operate a private cellular phone network.

Zimbabwe's independent Financial Gazette newspaper published on Thursday a letter it said was written by Vice-President Joshua Nkomo instructing Information, Posts and Telecommunications Minister Joyce Mujuru to carry out the president's order.

"His Excellency, the President of the Republic of Zimbabwe, Comrade R.G. Mugabe, has agreed and directed me to inform you that Econet, a company owned by Mr Strive Masiyiwa, must be licensed as one of the three GSM (Global System Module) cellular operators in Zimbabwe," Nkomo is quoted as saying in the letter.
Mujuru said she had not seen the letter, and would only issue a licence according to procedures laid down by the government tender board.
Masiyiwa declined to comment in detail on this development, but said he had been assured by "the highest office in the land" that he would get a licence.

Masiyiwa has been backed by the courts in his bid for a licence but has not been given one because the government kept changing the rules. Last week he withdrew his latest court challenge on the understanding he would be awarded a licence.
One cellular phone network licence was awarded to the state-owned Posts and Telecommunications (PTC) last year, and two more are at stake.

Three years ago Masiyiwa's Econet was the only company fighting for a private licence, after winning a constitutional challenge that the PTC's monopoly in the phone industry contravened basic human rights to choice and to information. Several other companies have since joined the race.
Mujuru's ministry has shortlisted four companies as possible operators, placing at the top Telcell, a consortium of local businesses and a foreign firm, and Econet at the bottom.
Mugabe's nephew, Leo Mugabe, is one of the partners in Telcell.

Many local economic and political analysts saw the the move as aimed at denying Masiyiwa a licence because he had allegedly refused to enlist some powerful political leaders as partners in the proposed business.
The Financial Gazette reported last week that Vice-President Nkomo had threatened to resign if government continued to deny Masiyiwa a licence and to act in a "criminal manner".
In a strongly worded commentary on Thursday, the weekly newspaper said Masiyiwa deserves a licence because he has already laid an infrastructure and is ready to switch on.
It said the shambles surrounding the bids for the cellular phone networks was a clear indication that the government must operate a transparent tender system.

"The ghosts of the government's bungling and ineptitude in handling its multi-billion dollar tenders have risen to torture its conscience, stripping the tender system of all pretensions that it is anything but flawed and, at worst, a vehicle for the powerful in Zimbabwe's society to enrich themselves and their cronies," the newspaper commented.
